papers.title: Tradición pública y conocimiento secreto en Ireneo de Lyon: memoria, sucesión episcopal y criterios de verdad en Adversus haereses
papers.title_ja: リヨンのイレナイオスにおける公開伝統と秘密知識：記憶、司教継承、『異端論駁』における真理の基準
papers.summary: Este artículo analiza la oposición entre tradición pública y conocimiento secreto en Ireneo de Lyon, especialmente en Adversus haereses. Desde un enfoque histórico-discursivo, se examina cómo Ireneo formula criterios de verdad frente a determinadas corrientes gnósticas del siglo II, no solo por medio de la refutación doctrinal, sino mediante la memoria apostólica, la sucesión episcopal, la regla de la fe y el carácter público de la transmisión eclesial. Se sostiene que la controversia ireneana no puede reducirse a una disputa teológica interna, sino que constituye una operación de legitimación histórica y comunitaria en un cristianismo plural y todavía no plenamente institucionalizado. El trabajo muestra que, para Ireneo, la verdad se presenta como tradición verificable en la continuidad pública de las iglesias, frente al carácter reservado, fragmentario y no contrastable del conocimiento secreto atribuido a sus adversarios.

papers.summary: In this transformative study, Simon Smith explores how playwrights like Shakespeare crafted their plays for demanding and varied commercial audiences. Rediscovering the many forms of judgement practiced in the early modern playhouse, he investigates influences ranging from the classical tradition and grammar-school classroom to ballad and jest culture. Where many prior studies have treated 'the judicious' as a self-contained subset of playgoers, Smith reveals the variety of careful assessments made in the theatre by a wide range of playgoers, showing that judgement and pleasure were often simultaneous elements of the same response. Chapters examine specific parts of plays that were especially subject to evaluation and generative of enjoyment: spectacle, words, plot, and actorly technique. papers.summary: Treating novel and film as thesis and antithesis, this chapter draws out ideas about breath in the novel and explores their transfer to the screen. It therefore seeks evidence of synthesis in how Zhao elicits meaning from camera movement and editing, choral music and breathing sounds, and a juxtaposition of close-ups with deep-focus wide and long shots that both simulates and stimulates breathing. Consequently, this analysis reinforces the theme of interconnectedness by consideration of the adaptation process as an exchange of energy between the novel and the film, by tracking descriptions of breathing in the novel and following this by analysing corresponding scenes in the film. Finally, this chapter explores how the link between ancient Daoist traditions of meditation and universal experiences of grief provides evidence of Zhao as an atemporal, transnational, peripatetic filmmaker.
